propositions.text: The claimant is a Sri Lankan citizen seeking refugee protection under IRPA subsections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: The claimant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Sri Lanka who seeks refugee protection pursuant to subsections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant is a Sri Lankan citizen seeking refugee protection under IRPA subsections 96 and 97(1).

propositions.text: The claimant fears return to Sri Lanka due to suspicion of LTTE affiliation, arrest, detention, and beatings in 2011.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges a fear in returning to Sri Lanka due to being suspected by authorities as being affiliated with LTTE, Liberation Tamil Tigers Eealam, a known terrorist group. The claimant was arrested, detained and beaten three separate times on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, XXXX XXXX, 2011 and XXXX 2011.

propositions.text: The claimant realized his life was at risk in 2011 and left Sri Lanka with his passport and an agent's help, arriving in Canada via the US.
propositions.quote: The claimant realized his life was at risk in XXXX 2011. The claimant departed Sri Lanka with his own passport and with the assistance of an agent and arrived in Canada via the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2011 and claimed refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges fear of return due to LTTE suspicion, arrests, and beatings in 2011, realized life risk, and fled to Canada with passport and agent help.

propositions.text: The claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

propositions.text: If returned, the claimant would not face personal risk to life or cruel and unusual treatment.
propositions.quote: The panel also finds that should the claimant return to Sri Lanka that he would not be subjected personally to a risk to his life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

propositions.text: There are no substantial grounds to believe the claimant would face torture if returned.
propositions.quote: Further, on substantial grounds, there is no danger of torture.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant is not a refugee or in need of protection and would not face risk or torture if returned.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, the claimant is a Sri Lankan citizen of Tamil ethnicity based on birth certificate evidence.
propositions.quote: On a balance of probabilities, the panel is willing to accept that the claimant is a citizen of Sri Lanka, who is Tamil in ethnicity, based on copies of his Sri Lankan birth certificate as seen in Exhibit R/A-2.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts on balance of probabilities that the claimant is a Sri Lankan Tamil citizen based on birth certificate evidence.

propositions.text: The key issue is the credibility of the claimant's evidence.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in this case is the credibility of the evidence as submitted.

propositions.text: Sellan case states a general credibility finding suffices unless independent credible evidence supports the claim; claimant bears onus.
propositions.quote: On the issue of credibility, the panel is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal case in Sellan3 which stated the following: Where the Board makes a general finding that the claimant lacks credibility, that determination is sufficient to dispose of the claim unless there is independent and credible documentary evidence in the record capable of supporting a positive disposition of the claim. The claimant bears the onus of demonstrating there was such evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states credibility is the key issue, guided by Sellan: general disbelief suffices unless independent credible evidence exists, claimant bears onus.

propositions.text: Federal Court says Board's credibility findings are factual and get high deference unless perverse or capricious.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Federal Court notes the following: The Board is in a much better position than a reviewing court to gage the credibility and plausibility of a refugee claimant's story. A credibility finding is not a finding of mixed fact and law. It is a finding of fact, pure and simple. Findings of fact made by the Board may only be interfered with by a reviewing court if the finding was made in a perverse or capricious manner or without regard for the material before it (see the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, paragraph 18.1(4)(d)). Indeed, it was Parliament's express intention that administrative fact-finding would command this high degree of deference (see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, [2009] S.C.J. No. 12 (QL) at paragraph 46). Thus, credibility findings of the Board are to be reviewed against the statutory standard of review provided for in paragraph 18.1(4)(d) of the Federal Courts Act (see Diabo v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 1772, [2004] F.C.J. No. 2168 (QL) at paragraph 3).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Federal Court law that Board credibility findings are factual and get high deference unless perverse or capricious.

propositions.text: Claimant fears return due to arrests and beatings linked to suspicion of LTTE affiliation via association with 'XXXX'.
propositions.quote: The evidence from the claimant resulting in his fear of return to Sri Lanka is due to being arrested, detained and beaten by the authorities due to the belief of the authorities that he is some how affiliated with the LTTE as the claimant played XXXX with a person, or in the same location of a person who is believed by the authorities to be associated with the LTTE.

propositions.text: Authorities questioned claimant about 'XXXX' believed linked to LTTE; claimant denies relationship beyond playing XXXX.
propositions.quote: The officials apparently questioned the claimant about a person known as "XXXX" who is also believed to have some connection with the LTTE. The claimant would deny any relationship with "XXXX", other than being known to the claimant as a consequence of playing XXXX.

propositions.text: Authorities disbelieved claimant; problems continued until claimant realized life risk in 2011 and left.
propositions.quote: The authorities, that being the army and CID did not believe the claimant and he continued to encounter problems until he realized his life was at risk in XXXX 2011 when he then made arrangements to leave the country.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts claimant's fear due to arrests linked to LTTE suspicion via 'XXXX', claimant denies ties, authorities disbelieved him until he fled.

propositions.text: Claimant does not know how authorities obtained information linking him to LTTE; only known link is via 'XXXX'.
propositions.quote: The panel asked the claimant if he knows what information the authorities had to believe the claimant was somehow affiliated with the LTTE. The claimant indicated that he did not know where they obtained their information from. Based on the evidence, it appears the only known link is via the person known as "XXXX".

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant unaware of how authorities linked him to LTTE; only known link is via 'XXXX'.

propositions.text: The panel considered claimant's profile and whether sufficient evidence exists of LTTE involvement or support.
propositions.quote: In trying to determine the likelihood of the claimant being suspected an affiliate of the LTTE, the panel considered the claimant's profile as a young Tamil male and whether there would be sufficient evidence that the claimant is involved or somehow supports the LTTE.

paragraphs.summary: The court considered claimant's profile and whether sufficient evidence shows LTTE involvement or support.

propositions.text: Evidence shows government brutality towards suspected LTTE affiliates and flawed investigations post-civil war.
propositions.quote: The evidence before this panel is replete with scathing reports about how government officials can be brutal towards persons it believes is involved with the LTTE. The panel notes the following from item 2.134 of the index: The aftermath of Sri Lanka's quarter century-long civil war, which ended in May 2009 with the defeat of the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), continued to dominate events in 2011. In April United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon released a report by a panel of experts that concluded that both government forces and the LTTE conducted military operations "with flagrant disregard for the protection, rights, welfare and lives of civilians and failed to respect the norms of international law." The panel recommended the establishment of an international investigative mechanism. Sri Lankan officials responded by vilifying the report and the panel members. The government has failed to conduct credible investigations into alleged war crimes by security forces, dismissing the overwhelming body of evidence as LTTE propaganda. The government's Lessons Learnt and Reconciliation Commission (LLRC), characterized as a national accountability mechanism, is deeply flawed, does not meet international standards for such commissions, and has failed to systematically inquire into alleged abuses. Despite the end of the formal state of emergency, the government also continues to hold several thousand people initially detained under the emergency regulations. Many have been held for years without trial, in violation of international law. The government has so far refused to even publish lists of those detained. The government has gradually released many, but not all, of the more than 11,000 suspected LTTE members detained at the end of the war and sent to so-called rehabilitation centers. The government denied detainees important due process guarantees, such as access to legal counsel, and thousands spent two years or more in detention. There are reports that some people released from the rehabilitation centers were harassed by security forces after they returned home.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes evidence of government brutality and flawed investigations against suspected LTTE affiliates post-civil war.

propositions.text: Claimant denies any LTTE affiliation and has no ties; only questioned in 2010 and 2011; heard of others questioned later.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked by the panel whether he was in any way affiliated with the LTTE. He responded in the negative. The claimant essentially has no ties with the LTTE. The claimant apparently was the only one questioned in XXXX 2010 and in XXXX 2011. The claimant did though hear that 2 others were questioned after XXXX 2011 but he had no information about their circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court records claimant denies LTTE ties, was questioned only twice, and heard of others questioned later.

propositions.text: It is difficult to believe claimant continued working for months if authorities suspected LTTE ties; negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: If and only if the claimant played cricket with someone who apparently has some connection or is believed to have some connection with the LTTE, it is difficult to believe that the claimant was able to continue working in a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX from XXXX 2010 until XXXX 2011 given such interests in him by the authorities. The panel does not believe his evidence and makes a negative credibility finding as a result.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's evidence not credible because he continued working despite alleged LTTE suspicion.

propositions.text: Claimant realized life risk in 2011 after last detention and alleged torture; claims beatings and suffocation during three-day detention.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked when he realized that his life was at risk. The claimant responded that he realized that his life was at risk in XXXX 2011 when he was last detained, beaten and tortured by the police. The claimant alleges he was beaten with pipes, with the hands of the authorities and suffocated while in detention for three days and then released.

propositions.text: If claimant was truly suspected LTTE affiliate, he would not have been released repeatedly or returned to work; negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: Again, if the claimant was such an interest to the authorities as alleged where he suffered, the panel does not believe the claimant would be released after each subsequent arrest and detention if he was truly suspected to be a LTTE affiliated. The panel also finds it difficult to believe that the claimant would then return to work for two more months until he was able to leave the country. The panel makes another negative credibility finding as a consequence.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes claimant's torture claims but finds them not credible given repeated releases and return to work.

propositions.text: Claimant testified he had to provide info on 'XXXX' within a month or be killed; no evidence he did so while living and working for two months.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the claimant testified that after his detention and release in XXXX 2011, he was required to provide the authorities with information about "XXXX", the other person the authorities were interested in and do so within one month of release or he would be killed. There is no indication the claimant gave the authorities information about "XXXX", which would allow him to avoid being killed by the authorities while working and living in the country for an additional 2 months before leaving.

propositions.text: The panel does not believe claimant's evidence about providing information and makes a negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: The panel does not believe his evidence in this regard and makes a negative credibility finding.

paragraphs.summary: The court disbelieves claimant's testimony about providing info on 'XXXX' and makes a negative credibility finding.

propositions.text: Item 13.15 describes government methods to find suspected LTTE affiliates including surveillance, arrests, profiling, and screening.
propositions.quote: The panel wishes to note item 13.15 of the index which provides some qualitative information about persons suspected of being LTTE affiliates or supporters. The document states: The methods for purging the "hidden" LTTE members who the government believes are still at large consist of "surveillance, arbitrary arrests and random check[s]," explains the Adjunct Professor (13 Jan. 2011). The second academic contacted by the Research Directorate, a York University law professor who is also a member of the advisory council of the Sri Lanka Campaign for Peace and Justice, somewhat similarly reports that Tamils throughout the country, particularly young Tamil men in the north or east, are being arrested and detained on suspicion of LTTE affiliation, a practice he describes as akin to "'ethnic' or 'racial' profiling" (Professor 20 Jan. 2011). The senior army officer reportedly told The New Yorker reporter that the army is building large military camps in the north and gathering intelligence with the help of spies in the Tamil population and electronic surveillance systems (The New Yorker 17 Jan. 2011, 49). The result of the government's efforts to find suspected Tigers is that screening is not limited to the IDP camps (Senior Research Fellow 28 Dec. 2010; Research Fellow 30 Dec. 2010). As the law professor explains, the government believes that "quite a number" of prominent LTTE figures remain at large and so is "very much on the look-out" for them (20 Jan. 2011). With the government still concerned with separating LTTE cadres from Tamil citizens, says the Senior Research Fellow, it is carrying out its screening in "residential areas all over the country" (28 Dec. 2010). According to the Research Fellow, screening is also being carried out at the airport (30 Dec. 2010). The law professor similarly says that he has it on good authority that the government is using "captured LTTE leaders as spotters at both the passport office in Colombo and at the airport" (20 Jan. 2011). He reports that the government is "routinely 'interview[ing]'" returned Tamil asylum seekers and, on what is "likely minimal standard[s]," arresting and detaining any who are suspected of being affiliated with the LTTE (Professor 20 Jan. 2011). He adds that Tamils flying into the Colombo airport who are not failed asylum claimants or deportees are also being "randomly screened and interrogated" (ibid.). Information corroborating the law professor's statement about the treatment of Tamils at the Colombo airport was not found among the sources consulted by the Research Directorate.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes item 13.15 describing government surveillance, arrests, profiling, and screening of suspected LTTE affiliates.

propositions.text: Claimant traveled from Northeastern Sri Lanka to Colombo by van with father and driver, passing 5-6 checkpoints without questioning.
propositions.quote: Given what the government does to locate suspected LTTE affiliates as well as using persons as spies, the panel asked the claimant how he was able to leave XXXX in the Northeastern area of the country to Colombo which is in the southern west location of the country. The claimant indicated that he traveled in a van as a passenger with his father and the driver to Colombo where they passed through approximately 5-6 checkpoints. The doors were opened when stopped and the claimant was seen but no questions were directed to him from the authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The court records claimant traveled by van with family through 5-6 checkpoints without being questioned.

propositions.text: Given alleged LTTE suspicion, it is unlikely claimant would pass checkpoints unchallenged; negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: Even if the driver who, according to the claimant spoke Sinhala to the authorities, given the alleged suspicion that the claimant is affiliated somehow with the LTTE, it would be reasonable to expect that the claimant would have been questioned or interrogated by the authorities to ensure his identity whether or not he had problems with the authorities in the past. This is not the case and it is difficult to believe this is so given the human rights violations committed by the authorities with a view of locating suspected LTTE affiliates. Again, the panel does not believe that the claimant is in any way of interest to the authorities or was believed to be a suspected LTTE affiliate. The panel makes another negative credibility finding as a result.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it unlikely claimant passed checkpoints unchallenged if suspected LTTE affiliate and disbelieves claimant's evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant's obtaining a passport and leaving via Colombo airport is not credible if he was suspected by authorities; negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the panel asked the claimant how he was able to obtain a passport issued in his own name in XXXX 2011 which is valid until XXXX 2021, given his alleged problems. The claimant indicated that he does not know how the agent obtained it for him. If the claimant is remotely on the radar of the authorities, regardless as to who applied for and obtained the passport, the panel does not see it credible, nor does the panel believe that the claimant would have been able to obtain a passport and successfully leave the country via the airport in Colombo with his passport. The panel makes a negative credibility finding as a result.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's obtaining a passport and leaving via airport not credible if suspected by authorities.

propositions.text: Claimant states authorities visited home 7-8 times asking about him; family said claimant left; authorities said they seek claimant due to 'XXXX'.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked if he had any information from his family about his situation today. The claimant stated that the authorities went to his home approximately 7-8 times asking about him. The claimant's father and or other relatives indicated that the claimant left XXXX. The authorities allegedly stated that "since he has connection to XXXX, we are looking for your son."

paragraphs.summary: The court records claimant's statement that authorities visited home multiple times seeking him due to 'XXXX'.

propositions.text: The court doubts claimant's connection to 'XXXX' or LTTE suspicion given his ability to work, pass checkpoints, obtain passport, and leave.
propositions.quote: The panel has difficulty believing the claimant has any connection with "XXXX" or is suspected by the authorities of being affiliated with the LTTE in a big or small way. If that was truly the case, the claimant would not likely be able to continue working after his alleged problems, would not likely be able to pass through 5-6 checkpoints undiscovered and would not likely be able to successfully obtain a passport in his own name in XXXX of 2011 and likely leave the country with the said passport if he was in fact wanted or of interest to the authorities in some way.

propositions.text: No credible evidence shows claimant's family suffered persecution due to claimant's situation or departure.
propositions.quote: Also, there is no credible indication that the claimant's family has suffered acts of persecution due to the claimant's situation and the claimant being lucky enough to successfully leave the country.

propositions.text: The panel disbelieves claimant's evidence and makes a negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: The panel does not believe the evidence as presented and makes a negative credibility finding.

paragraphs.summary: The court disbelieves claimant's connection to 'XXXX' or LTTE suspicion and finds no family persecution evidence.

propositions.text: Claimant fits profile of many Sri Lankan Tamil males accepted as refugees in Canada.
propositions.quote: he indicates that the claimant fits a profile similar to many Sri Lankan Tamil males who have been accepted in Canada as refugees

propositions.text: Claimant is of some interest to authorities, risking his life.
propositions.quote: the claimant is not a person that is of important interest to the authorities, but of some interest which would put the claimant's life at risk

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues claimant fits refugee profile and is of some interest to authorities risking his life.

propositions.text: Each case is assessed on its own merits; cannot find for claimant on profile alone.
propositions.quote: each case is assessed on its own merits and therefore it would not be appropriate to make a finding in favour of the claimant on this premise alone

propositions.text: Panel not persuaded claimant is of particular interest to authorities or has well-founded fear of persecution or life risk under section 97.
propositions.quote: the panel has not been so persuaded that the claimant is of particular interest to the authorities and therefore has a well founded fear of persecution or that his life is at risk pursuant to section 97 of the Act

paragraphs.summary: Court finds case must be assessed individually and claimant not shown to have well-founded fear or life risk.

propositions.text: Psychological assessment from Dr. XXXX dated XXXX 2012 is referenced as Exhibit C-2.
propositions.quote: psychological assessment as referenced in Exhibit C-2 from Dr. XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2012

propositions.text: Claimant assessed once by doctor; report based on claimant's information similar to Personal Information Form.
propositions.quote: information contained in the report comes from the claimant with evidence similar as that of the Personal Information Form

propositions.text: Psychologist diagnosed claimant with Major Depressive Episode and PTSD after one interview.
propositions.quote: psychologist summarizes that the claimant is presented with a "Major Depressive Episode and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder"

paragraphs.summary: Court notes psychological report diagnosing claimant with depression and PTSD based on one interview and claimant's info.

propositions.text: Psychological assessment is not persuasive that claimant suffers from these disorders due to Sri Lanka problems.
propositions.quote: information contained in the psychological assessment is not persuasive evidence for this panel that the doctor is in any position to state categorically that the claimant before it is suffering from "Major Depressive Episode and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder" as a result of the problems allegedly faced in Sri Lanka

paragraphs.summary: Court finds psychological assessment not persuasive that claimant's disorders result from Sri Lanka issues.

propositions.text: Psychiatric letters cannot cure all deficiencies in claimant's testimony (Rokni).
propositions.quote: a psychiatric/psychological letter submitted as evidence "cannot possibly serve as a cure-all for any and all deficiencies in a claimant's testimony"

propositions.text: Opinion evidence valid only if facts it is based on are true (Danailov).
propositions.quote: opinion evidence is only as valid as the truth of the facts on which it is based

propositions.text: Claimant may suffer mental illness but may not relate to described problems; psychological assessment given little weight.
propositions.quote: panel therefore gives little weight to the psychological assessment submitted for the panel's review

paragraphs.summary: Court cites precedent limiting psychiatric evidence and gives little weight to claimant's psychological assessment.

propositions.text: Section 97 requires persuasive evidence on balance of probabilities of substantial danger of torture (Li).
propositions.quote: pursuant to subsection 97(1) there must be persuasive evidence, that is on a balance of probabilities establishing the facts on which a claimant relies, to say that he or she faces a substantial danger of being tortured

propositions.text: Risk must be more likely than not to be tortured or subjected to cruel treatment (Li).
propositions.quote: the danger or risk must be such that it is more likely than not that he or she would be tortured or subjected to other cruel or other degrading treatments

propositions.text: This claim does not meet the section 97 standard for risk of torture.
propositions.quote: This is not the case in this claim

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Li requiring persuasive evidence of torture risk and finds claimant does not meet this standard.

propositions.text: Section 97 claims must consider all relevant factors and country's human rights record (Bouaouni).
propositions.quote: a claim under section 97 must be evaluated with respect to all the relevant considerations and with a view to the country's human rights record

propositions.text: Considering Sri Lanka's human rights record, claimant not shown to face substantial danger of torture or cruel treatment.
propositions.quote: the panel has not been persuaded that the claimant would face a substantial danger of being tortured, or that the risk and/or danger is such that it would be more likely than not

paragraphs.summary: Court applies Bouaouni, finds claimant not at substantial risk of torture considering Sri Lanka's human rights record.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to prove well-founded fear of persecution or need for protection clearly and convincingly.
propositions.quote: claimant has failed to meet his onus that he has a well founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground or that he is in need of protection in a clear and convincing fashion

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes claimant failed to prove well-founded fear or need for protection clearly and convincingly.

propositions.text: Claimant is not a Convention refugee; no reasonable chance of persecution, risk to life, or cruel treatment on return to Sri Lanka.
propositions.quote: the panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee as he has not established that there is a reasonable chance or serious possibility that he would be persecuted for a Convention ground or there would be a risk to his life or he would be subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment

propositions.text: Insufficient grounds to establish danger of torture; claim rejected under sections 96 and 97(1) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: there is insufficient grounds to establish danger of torture should the claimant return to Sri Lanka given the panel does not believe this claim as alleged. The panel rejects this claim pursuant to both sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects claim, finding no persecution or torture risk, under sections 96 and 97(1) of IRPA.
